device: offshore wind turbine blade leading edge
failure_mode: leading-edge rain and hail erosion of the composite blade skin
failure: Documented offshore wind reliability problem: the leading edge of rotating turbine blades (tip speeds commonly 75-90 m/s, offshore in wet and storm-heavy climates) suffers progressive rain and hail impact erosion of the gelcoat and composite laminate skin. Erosion roughens the surface, degrades aerodynamic performance (annual energy production loss reported in the range of several percent on affected fleets), can expose fibers, and forces early blade repair or replacement whose offshore crane and access-boat cost dominates the repair economics. Leading-edge protection solutions in service (polyurethane tapes, elastomeric coatings, metal erosion shields) trade added mass and step-height against erosion life and often fail by detachment or edge-lift themselves, partially at the tape/coating interface. This description is qualitative problem-domain context from the engineering literature; no specific incident statistics are asserted here (the engine's own retrieval must find and custody the evidence).
constraint: Any intervention must withstand continuous wet impact loading at blade tip speeds of 75-90 m/s for a design life of years, must not add enough mass at the blade tip to compromise blade root fatigue margins or turbine balance, must be installable on blades already in service offshore (limited access windows, no full blade replacement), and must not create a step or edge that trips the boundary layer or lifts in service.

sources.problem_basis: engineering-literature qualitative context; no fabricated incident counts
